props.title: The Tarnished Angels
props.initialSlug: Fallen WWI ace seeks glory in dangerous air shows

sections.content: Douglas Sirk's The Tarnished Angels (1957) represents a masterful adaptation of William Faulkner's "Pylon," capturing the gritty world of Depression-era barnstorming pilots with stark black-and-white CinemaScope photography. Unlike Sirk's better-known Technicolor melodramas like All That Heaven Allows (1955) and Written on the Wind (1956), this film strips away the glossy veneer to expose raw human desperation. Rock Hudson plays a cynical reporter drawn into the dangerous world of air show performers, anchored by Robert Stack's haunting portrayal of a WWI ace reduced to performing death-defying stunts and Dorothy Malone's complex role as his conflicted wife.

sections.content: The film's exploration of post-war disillusionment connects strongly to other aviation dramas like The Best Years of Our Lives (1946) and Twelve O'Clock High (1949), but Sirk brings a uniquely existential perspective. The carnival atmosphere of Depression-era air shows provides a backdrop for examining themes of mortality, fame's fleeting nature, and American mythmaking. Stack's character Roger Shumann embodies the lost generation of WWI veterans, unable to readjust to civilian life and addicted to the adrenaline rush of near-death experiences. SUBHEAD: Technical Innovation and Visual Style

Sirk and cinematographer Irving Glassberg use CinemaScope to spectacular effect, particularly in the thrilling air show sequences that still impress today. Their influence can be seen in later aviation films like The Right Stuff (1983) and The Great Waldo Pepper (1975). The film's stark visual style broke from Sirk's usual saturated colors, creating a documentary-like immediacy that heightens the story's tragic elements and social commentary. This approach influenced later New Hollywood directors, particularly in how they depicted Americana and disillusionment.
